channel.title: Sweet Escape Blog
channel.description: Frozen-dessert guides and shop updates from Sweet Escape in Memphis, Tennessee.

item.title: What Is a Marionberry? From Oregon Blackberry to Ice Cream
item.description: A marionberry is a named Oregon blackberry. Meet its two parents, see why researchers tasted it two ways, and follow it from pie to ice cream.

item.title: Can You Hear Crispness? The Science of a Crunchy Bite
item.description: What you hear can change how crisp a bite seems. Follow a headphone experiment, the sound of a wafer breaking, and a waffle chip into dessert.

item.title: Why Do Roasted Pecans Smell Different?
item.description: Roasting adds aromas a raw pecan doesn’t have. See what researchers found in the air above the nuts and why butter isn’t the only source of a buttery note.

item.title: Why Do Waffle Cones Have a Seam?
item.description: A waffle cone’s seam gives away how it was made. Follow a flat wafer from baking iron to rolling form, and see why the tip is a separate problem.

item.title: What’s Inside a Passion Fruit? Tiny Pockets of Juice
item.description: Passion fruit holds juice in sacs around its seeds. See where the tartness is concentrated and why dessert makers may strain the seeds or save them.

item.title: Why Does Ice Cream Shrink in the Freezer?
item.description: Ice cream can lose volume while it’s still frozen. See what happens to its air bubbles, why pressure matters, and how researchers measured the gap.

item.title: Why Does Frozen Yogurt Taste Tangy?
item.description: Frozen yogurt’s tang starts before the freezer. See how cultures make lactic acid, why milk thickens, and what changes when yogurt becomes dessert.

item.title: A Cactus Pear Isn’t a Pear. So What Is It?
item.description: Cactus pears grow on flat-stemmed cacti, not pear trees. Meet the fruit, its tiny barbs, and the ingredient behind a familiar ice cream name.

item.title: Why Does Vanilla Smell Sweet?
item.description: Vanilla aroma can change sweetness ratings, and sugar can strengthen vanilla flavor. Explore the two-way science behind a familiar frozen-dessert pairing.

item.title: Hazelnuts Can Wait Months After Pollination
item.description: Hazelnut flowers can receive pollen long before fertilization. Explore tiny red flowers, waiting pollen tubes, and the hidden calendar behind hazelnut gelato.

item.title: Why Does a Coconut Have Three Eyes?
item.description: A coconut has three eyes, but its sprout normally uses one. Follow the hidden embryo, coconut water, white kernel, and the sponge that grows inside.

item.title: Why Is Dutch-Process Cocoa Darker?
item.description: Dutch-process cocoa can darken without added sugar. See what researchers measured, how to read the label, and why one ice cream recipe uses two chocolates.

item.title: Why Does Ice Melt Faster on Metal That Feels Cold?
item.description: Room-temperature metal can feel cooler than plastic yet melt ice faster. A simple test shows why, and what changes when the ice is an ice cream scoop.

item.title: Why Do Peaches Have Fuzz but Nectarines Don’t?
item.description: A nectarine is a smooth-skinned peach. Find out what peach fuzz is, why scientists shaved peaches, and what the skin tells you about a frozen dessert.

item.title: Why Did Ice Cream Once Look Like George Washington?
item.description: A Memphis museum has a mold for George Washington ice cream. See how dessert makers shaped frozen portraits, dolphins, and even a Statue of Liberty.

item.title: Why Can Cool Weather Make Blood Oranges Redder?
item.description: Why do blood oranges turn red? See how cool conditions affect their pigments, how Cara Cara differs, and where sorbetto fits into the story.

item.title: Why a Cinnamon Roll Swirl Isn’t an Ice Cream Ripple
item.description: A cinnamon roll is a sliced spiral, but an ice cream ripple can start as a moving stream. Explore both shapes and Sweet Escape’s Cinnamon Roll Sundae.

item.title: Does Pumpkin Pie Need a Carving Pumpkin?
item.description: Pie pumpkins do not always look like jack-o’-lanterns. Explore squash species, canned pumpkin labels, and Sweet Escape’s Pumpkin Pie ice cream.

item.title: Why Can Ice Cream Feel Sandy?
item.description: Ice cream can feel sandy when milk sugar forms crystals. Learn how lactose differs from ice, what researchers measured, and why particle size matters.

item.title: The Ice Cream Stick Had a Job Before You Held It
item.description: Early ice cream bars and ice pops used their sticks for more than eating. Original patents reveal how the handles helped with coating and mold release.
